blocks.text: That there is a certain likeness between the sharp, toothed jaws of locusts and the jaws of lions, which the prophet has in view in this comparison, is observed by C. Guil. Iusti in the notes appended to his vernacular translation of Joel, from Fabricius, Genera Insectorum, p. 96.
So also the Syriac, ܠܡܫܘܚܠܐ, for tearing apart, and the Arabic in the Polyglots, للتفسيخ [li-l-tafsīkh], for rending.

All this is confirmed by Shaw, Travels p. 165. 166, German trans., where he describes at length the devastation brought upon the regions of North Africa by locusts. Moreover, [III, 297] as regards the interpretation of the word שריגים, rendered by some branches, by others vine-shoots, I add the words of Ed. Pococke in his Commentary on Joel p. 34, Latin trans.: “Abu Walid compares this word with the Arabic root سرغ [s-r-gh], which is used of leaves and branches انا امتدت [anā imtaddat] when they stretch themselves out. The foremost lexicographer of the Arabs, the author of the Qamus (Firuzabadi), says that the noun سرغ [sargh] means قضب الكرم للغض لسنته [quḍub al-karm li-l-ghaḍḍ li-sanatihi], the tender little branches of the vine of the first year, or كل قضيب رطب [kull qaḍīb raṭb], any moist (or green) rod. He likewise tells us that السرغ [al-sargh] alsargo, joined with غ g (which in sound differs little from the Hebrew), is قضيب الكرم [qaḍīb al-karm], the rod (or branch) of the vine.”

That they rendered ἐσκίρτησαν [eskirtēsan], I think the reason was not that they read בעטו for עבשו, as Cappellus conjectured, Crit. S. vol. II, p. 631, Vogel-Scharfenberg edition (a conjecture in which he has a follower in I. D. Michaelis, Supplemm. vol. VI, p. 1825); nor פשו, having grown fat they behaved foolishly, as I. Fr. Fischer would have it in Proluss. de Verss. Graecc. Librr. V. T. p. 13; nor פשו, they leap, which seemed probable to Scharfenberg on Cappellus, loc. cit.; but rather that they took the Hebrew עבש in the sense of playing, which belongs to the Arabic عبث [ʿabath], which is the view of Ed. Pococke in his Commentary p. 84, Latin trans.; or that they compared עבש with أفز [afaza], to leap up, which is the less probable opinion of Boysen, in a book written in the vernacular entitled Beyträge zu einem richtigen System der Hebräischen Philologie, vol. I, p. 342. That the Alexandrian and the Syriac translators read פרות in their manuscripts instead of פרדות, Mercerus, Cappellus, Fischer, Michaelis and others infer from the fact that the former put δαμάλεις [damaleis], the latter ܥܓ̈ܠܐ, calves. To these they also add the Latin Vulgate, which renders jumenta [beasts of burden], although to some it seems to have read the word with the same consonants but not the same vowels: as if it had formed a plural from פרדה, the feminine of the noun פרד, mule; one kind of beast being named, under which the other beasts of similar nature, or young animals in general, are included. Finally, Fischer concludes that instead of what we read today, מגרפתיהם, the Greek Alexandrian translator [III, 300] found in his manuscript הרפתיהם, from the fact that he rendered ἐπὶ ταῖς φάτναις αὐτῶν [epi tais phatnais autōn]; and רפתים is in another passage too (Habac. III, 17.) called φάτναι [phatnai] by the same translators. Mercerus, however, in his commentary on this passage, thinks that both this Greek rendering, ἐπὶ ταῖς φάτναις αὐτῶν [epi tais phatnais autōn], at their mangers or in their stalls, and the Latin Vulgate, in stercore suo [in their dung], rest above all on deriving the word from the root גרף, in so far as it denotes to sweep away, because dung is swept away from under the cattle, or out of their stalls.

These Chaldee words are more correctly rendered in Latin in the Polyglot Bibles thus: the wine-jars have rotted under their lids. This interpretation is confirmed by the authority of Abu Walid, the most learned grammarian of the Hebrews, cited by Ed. Pococke here as often (p. 80), who explains the words of the Chaldee translator thus: خبجت دنان الخمر وعفنت من طول مكثها فارغة [khabijat dinān al-khamr wa-ʿafinat min ṭūl makthihā fārigha] the wine-jars stink, or become rancid and musty, because they remain empty so long. It is clear that the Chaldee translator took the verb עבש in the sense of growing musty, rotting, which belongs to the Chaldee עפש, cognate in sound. The other Hebrew words, however, which he seems not to have understood well enough, he rendered by a free paraphrase.

ܥܒܫ ܥܓܠܬܐ ܥܠ ܐܘܪܝܘܬܗܝܢ, words which the Latin translator in the Polyglots renders thus: the heifers remained unfed at their mangers. But Ed. Pococke, p. 80. 82, notes that the verb ܥܒܫ is more correctly rendered they are parched or scorched, so that the more usual meaning of the Syriac ܥܒܫ is retained, and that the Syriac translator expressed the notion of being dry, which belongs to the Arabic عبس [ʿabasa], agreeing in spelling and sound with the Hebrew עבש. Cf. our note 11 below. That parched or dried-up heifers are heifers wasted by hunger scarcely needs pointing out.
